## What it is

The line comes from a post on ancestor worship in academia, about which fields treat their leading figures as heroes. Gelman notes "the habit of economists describing other economists in heroic terms", which he thinks economics took from mathematics and physics, and contrasts it with political science, where modern scholars "don't seem to be idolizing the political scientists of the mid and late twentieth century." Then: "Some more examples from economics are the extravagant and, in my impression, unreasonable adulation given to Gary Becker and Lawrence Summers. I'm sure these guys were impressive, but I don't think the whole thing of treating them as geniuses worked out so well. In a dark room with many of the lights covered up by opaque dollar bills, even a weak and intermittent beam can appear brilliant, if you look right at it."

He wonders whether part of the problem is that economics "has traditionally been taught as a history of great men as much as a history of ideas", and his conclusion applies to statistics too: "We should be able to celebrate great work without idealizing the individuals involved. They're just people!" Gelman doesn't spell out the image. Our reading: when money and prestige cover up the other lights, the few left in view look brighter than they are.

## Why it matters

Perceived excellence is *relative to what is visible*. When funding, gatekeeping or tradition hides alternative ideas, methods or people, mediocre work can look outstanding simply because there is nothing to compare it with. Judging quality requires asking what the room would look like with the bills removed.

## How it works

A toy model. Each idea has a true brightness. An observer sees the focal idea plus only the uncovered fraction $v$ of the others, and judges the focal idea by its rank among what is visible. As $v$ falls, a mediocre idea's *perceived* percentile rises, even though its true brightness hasn't changed.

## Simulated example

There are 200 ideas in a field, and the focal one is truly middling, at the 40th percentile. Cover up more and more of the alternatives and watch its apparent standing.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
import {rng, range, pct} from "../js/stats.js"
```

```{ojs}
viewof truePct = Inputs.range([0.05, 0.95], {value: 0.4, step: 0.05, label: "True percentile of the focal idea"})
viewof favored = Inputs.range([0, 1], {value: 0.7, step: 0.05, label: "How much covering favors weaker rivals"})
viewof seed = Inputs.range([1, 500], {value: 140, step: 1, label: "Random seed"})
```

```{ojs}
room = {
  const r = rng(seed);
  const others = r.normals(199).sort((a, b) => a - b);
  const focal = others[Math.floor(truePct * 198)];
  return range(20).map(k => {
    const visible = 1 - k * 0.05;
    let sum = 0;
    for (let rep = 0; rep < 200; rep++) {
      // Covering hits brighter rivals harder (they threaten the incumbent).
      const c = 1 - visible;
      const seen = others.filter(v => r() >= Math.min(1, c * (v > focal ? 1 + favored : 1 - favored)));
      sum += seen.length ? seen.filter(v => v < focal).length / seen.length : 1;
    }
    return {visible, apparent: sum / 200};
  });
}
```

```{ojs}
Plot.plot({
  ariaLabel: "In a dark room with many of the lights covered up by opaque dollar bills: simulation chart",
  ariaDescription: "Horizontal axis: Share of rival lights left uncovered. Vertical axis: Share of visible rivals the focal idea outshines. The chart updates with the controls above it, and the summary below the charts states the result in words.",

  ]
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
html`<div class="sim-readout">${md`The focal idea truly outshines **${pct(truePct)}** of its rivals (dashed line). With every light visible, it outshines **${pct(room[0].apparent)}** of what you can see. With most of the room covered, it appears to outshine **${pct(room.at(-1).apparent)}**. The beam didn't get brighter. The room got darker.`}</div>`
```

## R {.unlisted}

```{.r}
# In a dark room with most lights covered, a weak beam looks brilliant.
true_pct <- 0.4 # true percentile of the focal idea # <1>
favored <- 0.7 # how much the covering favors weaker rivals
set.seed(140) # <2>

others <- sort(rnorm(199)) # brightness of 199 rivals
focal <- others[floor(true_pct * 198) + 1] # a middling idea # <3>
visible <- 1 - (0:19) * 0.05 # share of rivals left uncovered # <4>
apparent <- sapply(visible, function(vis) {
  cover <- pmin(1, (1 - vis) * ifelse(others > focal, 1 + favored, # <5>
    1 - favored
  ))
  mean(replicate(200, {
    seen <- others[runif(199) >= cover]
    if (length(seen)) mean(seen < focal) else 1
  }))
})

cat("Truly outshines ", round(100 * true_pct), "% of rivals; appears to ",
  "outshine ", round(100 * apparent[1]), "% with every light visible and ",
  round(100 * apparent[20]), "% with most covered\n",
  sep = ""
)

plot(visible, apparent, # <6>
  type = "l", lwd = 3, col = "#b8860b",
  xlim = c(1, 0.05), ylim = c(0, 1),
  xlab = "Share of rival lights left uncovered",
  ylab = "Share of visible rivals it outshines"
)
abline(h = true_pct, lty = 2)
```
1. The page's controls: the focal idea's true percentile, and how much the covering favors weaker rivals over stronger ones.
2. Fixes the random numbers so the run is reproducible.
3. A middling idea among 199 rivals.
4. Cover up more and more of the rival lights.
5. Brighter rivals are more likely to be covered than dimmer ones: that is what the dollar bills do.
6. The share of visible rivals the focal idea outshines, as the room darkens. The dashed line is its true standing.

## Python {.unlisted}

```{.python}
# In a dark room with most lights covered, a weak beam looks brilliant.
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

true_pct = 0.4  # true percentile of the focal idea
favored = 0.7   # how much the covering favors weaker rivals
rng = np.random.default_rng(140)

others = np.sort(rng.normal(size=199))  # brightness of 199 rivals
focal = others[int(true_pct * 198)]     # a middling idea
visible = 1 - np.arange(20) * 0.05      # share of rivals left uncovered
apparent = []
for vis in visible:
    cover = np.minimum(1, (1 - vis) * np.where(others > focal, 1 + favored,
                                               1 - favored))
    shares = []
    for _ in range(200):
        seen = others[rng.uniform(size=199) >= cover]
        shares.append((seen < focal).mean() if seen.size else 1)
    apparent.append(np.mean(shares))

print(f"Truly outshines {100 * true_pct:.0f}% of rivals; appears to outshine "
      f"{100 * apparent[0]:.0f}% with every light visible and "
      f"{100 * apparent[-1]:.0f}% with most covered")

plt.plot(visible, apparent, color="#b8860b", linewidth=3)
plt.axhline(true_pct, color="black", linestyle="--")
plt.xlim(1, 0.05)
plt.ylim(0, 1)
plt.xlabel("Share of rival lights left uncovered")
plt.ylabel("Share of visible rivals it outshines")
plt.show()
```

## Key takeaways

::: takeaways
- Reputations are relative to the alternatives people can see.
- Hiding alternatives with money, gatekeeping or tradition makes mediocre work look brilliant.
- Before revering a figure or idea, ask what has been kept out of view.
:::
